key_facts: **Emollients** restore the skin barrier: the foundation of treatment for eczema, psoriasis, ichthyosis and dry skin.
Types run from lotions (light, more water) through creams and gels to **ointments** (greasiest, most occlusive, fewest preservatives).
Use **liberally and often**: adults with eczema may need about 250–500 g a week; apply in the direction of hair growth.
Use as a **soap substitute**; leave 15–30 minutes between emollient and topical steroid.
**Fire risk**: paraffin-based (and other) emollients dried on fabric are flammable; warn about naked flames and smoking (MHRA).

sections.title: Overview
blocks: Moisturisers that soften and hydrate the stratum corneum.

ul: **Occlusives** (paraffins, petrolatum, dimeticone) reduce transepidermal water loss.
**Humectants** (urea, glycerol, lactic acid) draw water in.
**Emollient lipids** (ceramides, oils) fill gaps in the barrier.

blocks: Formulations range from light lotions/gels → creams → greasy ointments, which work best and contain the least preservative. They are used as **leave-on** treatments, as **soap substitutes**, and (now rarely) as bath additives.

ul: **"Emollients are just moisturisers, optional"**: regular use reduces flares and steroid use.
**"Aqueous cream is a good emollient"**: it contains sodium lauryl sulfate, an irritant; avoid as a leave-on.

sections.title: How it works (mechanism of action)
blocks: Emollients work by **occluding, humectant attraction of water and replacing lipids**.

mech.t: Oily layers (paraffin, petrolatum) slow transepidermal water loss.
mech.caption: A leaky barrier loses water and lets irritants in; emollients seal it.

mech.t: Urea, glycerol and lactic acid draw water into the stratum corneum.
Ceramides and fatty acids refill gaps between corneocytes.
More oil = more occlusion but less cosmetic acceptability.
mech.caption: Spectrum from light lotions to greasy ointments.

mech.t: Smooth on downwards in the direction of hair growth to avoid folliculitis.
mech.caption: Apply in long downward strokes.

sections.title: Clinical features
blocks: Emollients restore the lipid "mortar" between corneocytes. They reduce water loss, irritant/allergen penetration and itch, and have a **steroid-sparing** effect (fewer flares, less steroid needed). In atopic eczema, filaggrin loss and soap/surfactant exposure drive barrier failure (see the [eczema](condition:eczema-dermatitis) notes see *Vitamin D analogues, coal tar*).
Step 0 of every eczema, psoriasis and ichthyosis plan. Also xerosis in older people, hand dermatitis and dryness after isotretinoin.

ul: **"The best emollient is the one the patient will use."** Offer 2–4 to try (sample packs or self-selection, photo C03). Consider dryness, site, time of day, school/work, preference and **allergens/irritants**: avoid **fragrance**, and check for **lanolin** (wool alcohols), **SLS**, **methylisothiazolinone** and preservatives in creams.
**Quantity check:** NICE CG57 — **250–500 g/week** for children; about **500 g/week** for adults with widespread dryness. A patient collecting one 500 g tub every 3 months is under-using.
Prescribe enough for **home and nursery/school** (NICE CG57).

ul: **Prescribe generously** (250–500 g/week for a child; ~500 g for an adult), in **pump dispensers** to reduce contamination, with a separate tub for the soap substitute.

**How to apply:** smooth on in the direction of hair growth (reduces folliculitis), often (at least 2–4 times daily and after washing), including when the skin is clear. Leave a gap between emollient and steroid.

**MHRA safety:** **Fire risk** with **both paraffin-containing and paraffin-free** emollients that dry onto clothing, bedding or dressings (DSU Dec 2018; reinforced 2020). Advise no smoking or naked flames; washing fabrics at high temperature may not remove all residue; tell carers and care homes; **Slips** in the bath/shower with emollient bath additives. Bath additives add no benefit (BATHE trial), and NICE CG57 (updated 2023) no longer advises offering them routinely
**Aqueous cream** (MHRA DSU 2013): may irritate the skin, particularly in children with eczema, probably because of SLS.
Fully within community/primary-care IP and OTC practice. Follow ICB self-care/formulary policies; many ICBs expect OTC purchase for mild dry skin.

fig.caption: Smooth emollient on in long strokes along the direction of hair growth; rubbing hard against it can block follicles and cause folliculitis.
fig.alt: Hand applying cream along the forearm

ladder.t: **Pump dispensers**; separate tub for soap substitute. Generous quantities (as above).
Smooth on **in the direction of hair growth** (less folliculitis). At least **2–4 times daily** and after washing, even when clear.
**Fire risk** with paraffin and paraffin-free emollients on clothing, bedding, dressings: no smoking or naked flames; tell carers. **Slips** with bath additives; BATHE trial: no added benefit.

blocks.title: Prescribing limits and pitfalls
list: **Fire**: Residue on fabric burns easily; washing may not remove it.

refer.t: Uncontrolled despite adequate emollient + TCS: refer per NICE CG57.
Suspected emollient contact allergy: patch testing.
Erythroderma or infected eczema: assess promptly.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: Warn about **fire risk**: dressings, clothing and bedding soaked in any emollient (paraffin or paraffin-free) can catch fire easily (MHRA).
Eczema still uncontrolled despite adequate emollient + TCS (see NICE CG57 referral criteria); suspected emollient contact allergy (patch testing); erythroderma; infection.
Folliculitis, irritant reactions (preservatives, lanolin), slipping and falls, fire risk.
Ongoing, lifelong in chronic conditions.

pearls: "Emollients are the treatment, not an extra."
Show the FTU *and* a handful of emollient. For a child with widespread eczema, a 500 g tub should last about a week.
Fire-safety counselling is an MHRA expectation — record that you gave it.

quiz.q: Weekly emollient for a child with eczema (NICE)?
Why not aqueous cream as a leave-on?
quiz.a: Contains SLS: stinging and barrier damage (MHRA 2013).
In the direction of hair growth, to reduce folliculitis.

quiz.q: Fire risk applies to which emollients?
quiz.a: Both paraffin-containing and paraffin-free products soaked into fabric.
